# Will I Miss It?

> "What fruit then did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed?"
>
> — Romans 6:21

No.

The Little Monster starves, and the grooves the habit wore into your evenings grow over. The last scraps of the old lies go with them. You'll handle a hard day better than you do now. And the good days will be properly good, because you'll be there for the whole of them, with nothing to hide when you get home.

Paul didn't ask the Romans what they'd lost. He asked what they ever got. Go on, answer it. What fruit?

The fear of missing it is very old. Augustine, on the edge of his own freedom, heard his old habits pleading with him. They "plucked my fleshy garment, and whispered softly, 'Dost thou cast us off? and from that moment shall we no more be with thee for ever?'" That whisper is all the trap has left at the end: *never again? Not even once?* It's made out to be a loss. He walked out anyway, and never wrote a line about missing them.

There's only one real danger left, and it's other men.

## The greener grass {-}

Everybody thinks the next field is greener. That's normal when the next field has something in it. Here it's baffling. On one side: a clear head, a clean conscience and your evenings back. On the other: ten minutes, a tissue and a sinking feeling. So why would a free man ever look over the fence with envy?

Because the world never stops telling him he's the odd one. Sitcoms treat the habit as a harmless joke and "experts" call it healthy. Then one night you're on your own, a bit low, a bit lonely (being single is no crime, by the way), and the thought arrives: *Everyone else gets to. Why not me?*

Look at how strange that thought is. Every man who never picked the habit up is glad he didn't. Every man who still has it wishes he'd never begun, and he'll tell you so after a couple of honest questions. Not one of them recommends it to his son. So who exactly are you envying?

## Watch him closely {-}

The envy only works if you picture a single occasion: one warm, private, harmless little time. That occasion doesn't exist. There is only the whole chain, and the man chained to it.

So picture him instead. Better still, remember him, because nobody knows him better than you do.

He doesn't settle down to it like a man sitting down to a good dinner. He drifts into it. The phone is already in his hand before he's decided anything. He flicks from one thing to the next, and nothing he finds is quite right. If there's no screen, he rifles through the same worn memories. He's hurrying. He's half listening for the door. When it's over he lies there flat and slightly sick of himself, and makes the usual promise. In the morning he gets up tired, with one more broken promise on his record.

Did that look like fun to you? He isn't enjoying himself. He's a man who has lost the ability to enjoy an empty evening without it. And he has the same thing booked for tomorrow, the day after, and every stressful Tuesday for the rest of his life. For what?

He doesn't approve of himself. If he knew you'd walked out, HE WOULD ENVY YOU.

## Who is doing without? {-}

The other reason a free man gets a twinge is simpler. The other fellow is *doing* something and you aren't, so it feels as if you're the one going without.

Turn it the right way up. You're not going without anything. He is. He is going without:

- Energy
- Drive
- Confidence
- A clear conscience
- Closeness to God
- Freedom
- Self-respect
- A word he can keep

He can't trust himself. You can.

Ask the men who've been out for a while whether they pine for it. One of them, hooked from twelve to twenty-one, wrote:

> "I've been freed now and it's nearly been 7 years."
>
> — a man on a Christian forum

He says his freedom came when God met him, and he describes what came with it: "this truly sensational feeling of peace for the first time in my life". That doesn't sound like a man missing his old hobby. A coach on YouTube, eighteen months out, was blunter: "there is no downside", and "i'm never going back".

So drop the habit of envying men who are still in the trap. I'm not sneering. I was one of the worst. You wouldn't envy a man who can't get through the day without a drink, however cheerfully he raises his glass. And like every trap of this kind, it doesn't stand still. It tightens. If he isn't enjoying it this year, he'll enjoy it less next year.

Don't envy him. Pity him, pray for him, and when the chance comes, hand him this book.
